# Compactness and attained minima for the joint planar cap-section problem

This note supplies an actual boundedness and attainment argument for an
ordinary planar variational problem. It does not determine the attained
minimum or prove that an attaining body is a triangle.

Fix finitely many nonzero normals u_1,...,u_N that positively span R^2:
their nonnegative cone is all of R^2. Let 0<c<1/2. For a convex body K
write

    k=|K|,
    q_i(K)=|K intersect {u_i.x>=0}|.

The cap constraints are q_i(K)<=c k for every i. The source is fixed
at 0. No translation normalization of K is permitted or needed.

## 1. The cap bound forces source interior

Every positive-area convex body satisfying these bounds has 0 in its
interior. If not, separation gives a nonzero n with K subset {n.x>=0}.
Positive spanning and conic Caratheodory in R^2 express n as a
nonnegative linear combination of at most two listed normals. For
completeness, start with any finite nonnegative representation and,
if more than two coefficients are positive, use a linear dependence
among those vectors to adjust the coefficients until one becomes
zero, preserving nonnegativity; repeat. The dependence may be given
the sign having a positive coefficient, so this elimination is valid.

If n=alpha u_i+beta u_j with alpha,beta>=0, then at every point of
{n.x>=0} at least one of u_i.x,u_j.x is nonnegative. Thus these two
closed caps cover K (one cap suffices if a coefficient is zero). Their
volumes sum to at least k, contradicting q_i+q_j<=2ck<k. This argument
includes source-boundary cases; no halfspace with positive boundary
measure is discarded.

## 2. An explicit radius bound

Set

    U=max_i ||u_i||,
    kappa=min_(e in S^1)
       min(max_i u_i.e, max_i(-u_i.e)),
    T=U/kappa.

The number kappa is positive. Positive spanning makes both maxima
strictly positive at every e; they are continuous on the compact unit
circle, so their minimum is attained and positive.

For EVERY feasible K,

    [max_(x in K)||x||]^2 <= 8T k/(1-2c).                         (1)

To prove it, let p=R e attain the maximal radius R, and take a unit
perpendicular e_perp. Write W for the width of K in that perpendicular
direction. Since 0 is interior, choose q_+,q_- in K with maximal and
minimal perpendicular projections, of opposite signs. The two triangles
conv(0,p,q_+) and conv(0,p,q_-) lie in K and have disjoint interiors
on opposite sides of the e-axis. Their total area is R W/2. Hence

    W<=2k/R.                                                     (2)

There are listed normals u_+,u_- with u_+.e>=kappa and
u_-.e<=-kappa. Every x in K has the form s e+t e_perp with |t|<=W,
because the projection interval of width W contains zero. Consequently
u_+.x>=0 whenever s>=TW, and u_-.x>=0 whenever s<=-TW. The two caps
therefore cover K outside the strip |e.x|<=TW. That strip's intersection
with K has area at most 2TW^2 by Fubini. Thus

    2ck>=q_++q_->=k-2TW^2>=k-8T k^2/R^2.

Rearranging proves (1). The same proof works if the strip is wider than
K; the displayed lower bound is then merely weak, not invalid.

This prevents long thin escaping bodies using the actual fixed cap
bounds. It is independent of a claimed stability modulus near a triangle.

## 3. Hausdorff compactness with the original source retained

Normalize k=1. Let F be the class of feasible convex bodies with any
additional CLOSED conditions on their finite cap-volume vector. For
example, with three normals one may impose the joint profile

    F_K=q_(1)+q_(2)+q_(3)/4<=1,

where the subscripts denote increasing order. Then F is Hausdorff
compact if nonempty.

By (1), every member lies in one fixed closed ball about the original
source. The Blaschke selection theorem for compact convex subsets of
a fixed compact ball supplies a Hausdorff-convergent subsequence from
any sequence. Equivalently, the support functions have one uniform
bound and Lipschitz constant, so a diagonal subsequence followed by
uniform approximation gives the same compact convex limit.

Let that limit be K. It cannot have zero area: if it did, the bounded
outer parallel neighborhoods K+epsilon B_2 would have areas tending
to zero, while eventually containing the area-one approximating bodies.
Thus K has interior. Indicators of convex bodies converging in Hausdorff
distance to a body with interior converge almost everywhere to its
indicator. Indeed exterior points are eventually outside; interior
points are eventually inside by an inner homothetic copy about any
fixed interior point. The boundary of a full-dimensional convex body
has area zero. Dominated convergence in the fixed containing ball
therefore gives

    |K|=1, q_i(K_l) tending to q_i(K) for every fixed cap i.

The cap upper bounds and every additional closed cap-vector condition
pass to K. Section 1 now gives 0 in int K. This last step is necessary:
source interior was not merely presumed to survive the limit.

## 4. Continuity and actual attainment of inverse-section objectives

Assume the cutting lines are fixed and put

    sigma_i(K)=H_1(K intersect {u_i.x=0})/||u_i||,
    lambda_i(K)=(1/sigma_i(K))/sum_j(1/sigma_j(K)).

All sigma_i are positive. They are continuous on F. To see this
directly, suppose K_l tends to K and let rho B_2 subset K be a ball
about 0. If their Hausdorff distance is epsilon_l<rho, support-function
inequalities give

    (1-epsilon_l/rho)K subset K_l
        subset (1+epsilon_l/rho)K.

Intersect with each fixed line through 0 and compare lengths. The
same two multiplicative factors sandwich sigma_i(K_l)/sigma_i(K),
proving its convergence. No section-limit assertion at a source
boundary is used.

Each lambda_i and min_i lambda_i is consequently continuous on the
compact class F. Therefore its minimum is actually attained whenever
F is nonempty. This conclusion is not a formal invocation of an
unproved extremal-body existence principle.

For the specific three normals (1,0),(0,1),(-1,-1), c=128/279, and
F_K<=1, nonemptiness is explicit. Scale the centered triangle
conv{(2,-1),(-1,2),(-1,-1)} to area one. Its three cap fractions are
4/9=124/279<c and its joint profile equals one. Thus the minimum in
the strengthened ordinary cap/section question is attained by at
least one actual convex body with the original source interior.

## 5. A structural consequence, not a triangle classification

The contact-star cut-and-fill theorem in
`candidate ace6d0d9c40d2c09`
applies to this class: its variations fix area and only decrease cap
coordinates, so all three cap bounds and F_K<=1 stay feasible.

At a minimizer of a specified lambda_i, each endpoint P of its central
section must therefore lie on a flat exposed face reaching another
cut line. Otherwise the contact-star theorem gives a nearby feasible
body with a strictly smaller lambda_i. This applies also to a minimizer
of min_i lambda_i, choosing an index i attaining that minimum there:
such a body also minimizes lambda_i, since every feasible lambda_i is
at least the global minimum of min_j lambda_j.

The attained minimum has NOT been shown to be >=2/9. Nor has its body
been shown to be a triangle or a polygon with a bounded number of
vertices. The two required face incidences are the current proved
restriction on that attained minimizer.

## 6. A quantitative interior ball

Write epsilon=1-2c>0, retain R and T from Section 2, and let
rho=min_(||n||=1) h_K(n). Section 1 gives rho>0, and rho is exactly
the radius of the largest ball centered at the original source and
contained in K. In addition to (1), one has

    rho >= epsilon k/(2R),
    rho^2 >= epsilon^3 k/(32T).                                  (3)

Choose a unit outward support normal n_0 with h_K(n_0)=rho, and
put n=-n_0. Then K lies in {n.x>=-rho}. Express n as a nonnegative
combination of at most two listed normals, as in Section 1. Points
missing both corresponding closed caps satisfy n.x<0. Their area
is at least k-q_i-q_j>=epsilon k, but they lie in the strip
-rho<=n.x<0. Since K lies in the radius-R ball, Fubini bounds this
strip area by 2R rho. This proves the first inequality. Squaring and
using R^2<=8Tk/epsilon gives the second. If the representation uses
only one listed normal, its missing mass is even larger; the same
bound remains valid.

Thus the normalized feasible class has an explicit common inner
ball as well as an explicit common outer ball. In particular, no
unquantified limiting argument is needed merely to retain positive
central section lengths in this fixed-normal planar problem.
